openingProblem.problem: In 1960 the South African government banned the ANC and jailed its leaders. Thirty years later it unbanned the ANC and freed Mandela. Why did a regime that had crushed every challenge decide in 1990 to negotiate away white minority rule?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: what forced the apartheid government to negotiate?
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which piece of evidence most changed or confirmed it?

chunks.title: Apartheid: a racial state, 1948–1960
chunks.body:
Until 1994 South Africa was ruled by a white minority. Racial discrimination long predated apartheid. The Union of South Africa, created in 1910, gave the vote to all white men but allowed only whites into parliament, though whites were only 21 per cent of the population. The 1913 Land Act confined African land ownership to reserves covering less than a tenth of the country, and in 1936 Africans in the Cape lost the vote in general elections.

In 1948 an Afrikaner nationalist government, the **National Party**, came to power determined to go further. Its system of **apartheid** classified every South African into one of four "race groups": white, coloured, Indian and African. Schools, universities, hospitals, residential areas, transport, sports facilities, public amenities and even cemeteries were segregated, and those for "non-whites" were always inferior. A battery of laws enforced the system: the Population Registration Act recorded everyone's race; the Mixed Marriages Act and the Immorality Act banned relationships across racial lines; the Group Areas Act forced thousands from their homes.

Africans suffered most. The reserves were turned into "homelands", one for each "tribal" group, as part of a strategy of divide and rule, and millions were forcibly moved there. Every African had to carry a pass that restricted movement to the cities; urban Africans lived in poorly serviced townships. **Bantu Education** gave African children a separate curriculum designed, Bottaro and Stanley write, "to produce an uncritical, unskilled workforce". In 1956 coloured voters in the Cape lost the vote, ending a century-old tradition. From then on only whites had democratic rights.

This mattered because apartheid denied democratic rights to the great majority of South Africans by law, which meant that the demand for democracy in South Africa was inseparable from the struggle against racial oppression.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The Cape had a non-racial franchise tradition until 1956.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Apartheid classified and segregated every South African by race.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Its laws were enforced unevenly across regions.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Homelands, passes and Bantu Education entrenched inequality.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The government claimed homelands offered 'separate development'.

howItGetsAsked: Examine the nature of apartheid between 1948 and 1960.
To what extent was mass protest the main reason for the collapse of apartheid between 1976 and 1990?

useItInAnEssay.claim: Apartheid was a system designed to make racial inequality permanent by law.
useItInAnEssay.prove: From 1948 the Population Registration Act classified everyone by race, the Group Areas Act forced thousands from their homes, and Bantu Education aimed to produce an unskilled workforce.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that every part of life, from schooling to residence, was fixed by race, so Africans were confined to homelands and townships with inferior services.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, apartheid built on earlier discrimination, such as the 1913 Land Act, so it intensified rather than created white domination.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Apartheid was therefore the most systematic form of a racial order that had existed since the Union of 1910.

chunks.title: From protest to armed struggle, 1955–1976
chunks.body:
Resistance was as old as segregation. The **African National Congress** (ANC), founded in 1912, spent five decades using peaceful methods, including delegations to the British government, without success. After the Second World War its demands became more assertive. In 1955 the ANC and its allies drew up the **Freedom Charter**, setting out a vision of a democratic South Africa based on equality and non-racialism. It became the blueprint for the constitution the resistance hoped one day to write.

Peaceful protest failed to change government policy. In 1960 police opened fire on a crowd protesting against the pass laws at **Sharpeville**, killing sixty-nine people and injuring more than a hundred. The government banned the ANC and used increasing force against its opponents. The ANC set up its headquarters in exile and formed an armed wing, **Umkhonto we Sizwe** (MK, "Spear of the Nation"), to carry on underground resistance. Nelson Mandela and other MK leaders were arrested, found guilty of trying to overthrow the government and sentenced to life imprisonment.

By the mid-1960s the government seemed firmly in control. But a new generation emerged. Inspired by **Steve Biko's** Black Consciousness Movement, which promoted pride in black identity, students in Soweto protested in 1976 against inferior Bantu Education. In the **Soweto uprising** an estimated 1,000 people died. Thousands of young people left the country to train as MK guerrillas. Biko himself was murdered in police custody in 1977. The historian André Odendaal argues that the uprisings "forever changed the balance of power", and many historians see Soweto as the turning point after which the apartheid government never fully regained control.

This mattered because the failure of peaceful protest and the brutality of the state's response turned the struggle into an armed and mass movement, which meant that by the late 1970s apartheid faced both guerrilla warfare and a generation of young people who rejected it completely.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Freedom Charter defined the democratic goal.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Peaceful methods failed for five decades.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Sharpeville ended peaceful protest and led to armed struggle.
Soweto changed the balance of power.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The state still crushed the uprising in 1976.

useItInAnEssay.claim: The Soweto uprising was a turning point because it showed that a new generation could no longer be governed in the old way.
useItInAnEssay.prove: In 1976 students inspired by Black Consciousness protested against Bantu Education; an estimated 1,000 people died, and thousands left to train as MK guerrillas.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the armed struggle gained new recruits and the state lost its aura of invincibility, so Odendaal argues the uprisings 'forever changed the balance of power'.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the government crushed the uprising and banned Black Consciousness organisations, so apartheid survived for another fourteen years.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Soweto was therefore significant as the beginning of the end, rather than the end itself.

chunks.title: Reform, revolt and stalemate, 1976–1989
chunks.body:
After Soweto the state tried both repression and limited reform. It banned Black Consciousness organisations, allowed the police to detain suspects indefinitely without trial, spent huge sums on arms and conscripted every young white man for two years.

The most important reform was a new constitution in 1983. It created a **tricameral** (three-chamber) parliament, with separate houses for coloureds and Indians, while whites kept most of the power and Africans were excluded altogether. The government hoped to win coloured and Indian support. Instead the reform provoked mass protest. A non-racial **United Democratic Front** (UDF) was formed to oppose it and soon had about three million members; fewer than 20 per cent of coloured and Indian voters took part in the first tricameral elections in 1984. In 1985 the new black unions united in the Congress of South African Trade Unions (**COSATU**).

The exclusion of Africans enraged the townships, and from 1984 a sustained uprising began: rent boycotts, stayaways, consumer boycotts, school boycotts under the slogan "liberation before education", and street committees that took over local administration. The government declared a **state of emergency** and sent the army into the townships. Thousands were killed, but repression failed to crush the protests. For most of the 1980s, Bottaro and Stanley conclude, South Africa was in a state of virtual civil war.

In 1989 the UDF and COSATU formed the Mass Democratic Movement, which launched a nationwide defiance campaign. People ignored banning orders, opened segregated facilities and openly flew the flag of the banned ANC. Huge "Freedom Marches" filled the cities. The government, which had always used force against such protests, now did nothing.

This mattered because limited reform without African rights only intensified resistance, which meant that by 1989 neither repression nor reform could restore the government's control.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: It did give coloureds and Indians some representation.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The township uprising made South Africa ungovernable.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The state of emergency kept the regime in power.

argumentsThatWork.claim: By 1989 the government no longer used force against mass protest.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: It still controlled the army and police.

useItInAnEssay.claim: The tricameral constitution failed because it excluded the African majority while trying to divide the opposition.
useItInAnEssay.prove: It gave coloureds and Indians separate houses with little power, but the UDF, with about three million members, persuaded over 80 per cent of coloured and Indian voters to boycott the 1984 election.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the reform won no legitimacy, while the exclusion of Africans provoked a township uprising from 1984.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the reform did divide the regime's opponents for a time, and the state of emergency kept the government in power.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The constitution therefore failed because it reformed apartheid without ending it.

chunks.title: Why did change come in 1990?
chunks.body:
On **2 February 1990** President **F.W. de Klerk** told parliament that the ANC and other banned parties would be legalised, political prisoners released, the death penalty suspended and a democratic constitution negotiated. Shortly afterwards Nelson Mandela walked free. Why did change come then? Historians agree that several factors combined, but disagree about which mattered most.

**The armed struggle and isolation.** MK attacked high-profile targets such as the Sasolburg oil refinery and the Koeberg nuclear power station, supported by the "frontline states". South Africa had left the Commonwealth in 1961, was expelled from the Olympic Movement and suspended from the UN General Assembly, and faced sporting, cultural and academic boycotts. In 1988 South African forces were defeated by Cuban troops at Cuito Cuanavale in Angola, and the government accepted Namibian independence in 1990.

**The economy and sanctions.** In 1985 overseas banks cancelled loans and the rand collapsed. The US Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act of 1986 banned new investment, and about two-thirds of US companies with South African investments withdrew.

**The end of the Cold War.** Thatcher and Reagan had resisted sanctions, seeing the government as an anti-Communist ally; that justification now vanished, while the ANC lost Soviet backing. Nigel Worden sees the fall of the Berlin Wall as critical to the timing of De Klerk's announcement. Hermann Giliomee calls the loss of Soviet funding the "decisive factor in the ANC's abandonment of the revolutionary struggle". Francis Wilson disagrees: the end of the Cold War "facilitated the process of change ... but ... did not cause it".

**Mass protest and stalemate.** Chris Saunders believes the mass uprising of the 1980s was the most important factor. Leonard Thompson argues that by 1989 both sides accepted that neither could win militarily. De Klerk, who replaced P.W. Botha in 1989, was more open to reform, and the National Party believed it could control the negotiations. Contacts had already begun: Mandela had held secret talks with the government since 1985, while refusing any release with conditions attached ("Only free men can negotiate").

This mattered because no single factor forced the change, which meant that historians' judgements depend on whether they stress pressure from inside South Africa or the changing world outside it.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Internal mass protest made the country ungovernable.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Protest had been crushed before, in 1960 and 1976.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The economy and sanctions raised the cost of apartheid.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Thatcher and Reagan resisted sanctions for years.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The end of the Cold War decided the timing.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Wilson argues it facilitated but did not cause change.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Change came in 1990 because internal pressure and a changed world removed the government's options at the same moment.
useItInAnEssay.prove: The township uprising had made the country ungovernable, the 1985 debt crisis and 1986 US sanctions had weakened the economy, and the fall of the Berlin Wall ended the Cold War justification for apartheid.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that repression no longer worked and Western support had gone, so De Klerk, who replaced Botha in 1989, chose to negotiate on 2 February 1990.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, historians differ: Saunders stresses mass protest, Worden the fall of the Berlin Wall, and Wilson argues the end of the Cold War facilitated but did not cause change.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The timing was therefore set by the end of the Cold War, while the pressure for change came from inside South Africa.

modelPlan.thesis: The end of the Cold War was decisive for the timing of negotiations, as Worden and Giliomee argue, but it facilitated rather than caused the change, as Wilson argues: the pressure came from mass protest, the economy and military stalemate.

arguments.claim: For: the loss of Western and Soviet backing.
For: De Klerk's timing after the Berlin Wall.

modelPlan.counter: Secret talks with Mandela began in 1985, before the Cold War ended.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Cause or catalyst? A catalyst: it changed when, not whether.

segments.text: The end of the Cold War was the catalyst, not the cause, of the decision to negotiate.
Worden sees the fall of the Berlin Wall as critical to the timing of De Klerk's speech of 2 February 1990, and Giliomee argues the loss of Soviet funding pushed the ANC to negotiate.
This meant that both sides lost their Cold War backers, so the risks of negotiation fell for each.
However, Wilson argues it 'facilitated' but 'did not cause' change, and secret talks with Mandela had begun in 1985.
The claim is therefore valid for the timing, but the causes lay in South Africa itself.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Evaluate the significance of the Soweto uprising of 1976 in the struggle for democracy in South Africa.

decodeKey.verb: Evaluate: weigh strengths and limits, then judge
decodeKey.judgement: Turning point, or one stage among many?

modelPlan.thesis: Soweto was significant as the start of a shift in the balance of power, as Odendaal argues, because it fed the armed struggle and broke the myth of white invincibility; but the regime survived it for fourteen years.

arguments.claim: Later stages: the UDF and township uprising.

modelPlan.counter: The decisive pressure came only in the 1980s, with the UDF and the township uprising.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Was Soweto a turning point? Yes for the balance of power, no for the regime's survival in the short term.

segments.text: The Soweto uprising was a turning point in the struggle for democracy, though not its end.
Students inspired by Black Consciousness protested against Bantu Education; an estimated 1,000 died, and thousands left to train as MK guerrillas.
This meant that the armed struggle gained new recruits and the government lost its aura of invincibility, so Odendaal argues the uprisings 'forever changed the balance of power'.
However, the state crushed the uprising, and apartheid survived until the township revolt of the 1980s made the country ungovernable.
Soweto was therefore significant as the beginning of the end, rather than the end itself.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Examine the nature of apartheid between 1948 and 1960.

decodeKey.verb: Examine: break the issue into parts and consider their interrelationship

modelPlan.thesis: Apartheid was a comprehensive legal system that classified everyone by race, segregated every area of life and denied the majority political rights, building on and intensifying earlier discrimination.
modelPlan.counter: Apartheid intensified rather than created discrimination, which dated back to 1910 and 1913.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: How did the parts connect? Classification made segregation possible, and segregation justified political exclusion.

segments.text: Apartheid was a system that made racial inequality permanent by law.
The Population Registration Act classified everyone by race, the Group Areas Act forced thousands from their homes, and Bantu Education aimed to produce an unskilled workforce.
This meant that every area of life was fixed by race, so Africans were confined to homelands and townships and denied political rights.
However, apartheid built on earlier discrimination, such as the 1913 Land Act and the whites-only parliament of 1910.
Apartheid was therefore the most systematic form of an older racial order, completed when coloured voters lost the vote in 1956.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Examine the reasons for, and the results of, F.W. de Klerk's announcement of 2 February 1990.

decodeKey.verb: Examine: break the issue into parts and consider their interrelationship
decodeKey.judgement: Which reason mattered most, and which result was most significant

modelPlan.thesis: De Klerk acted because mass protest, economic decline and the end of the Cold War had closed the government's options, and because he believed the National Party could control negotiations; the result was the unbanning of the ANC, Mandela's release and the start of talks.

arguments.claim: Reason: the end of the Cold War.
Result: unbanning and release of prisoners.

modelPlan.counter: De Klerk believed he could control the process, which suggests he did not expect majority rule.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which result mattered most? The start of negotiations, which led to the 1994 election.

segments.text: De Klerk announced reform because the government's options had run out.
The township uprising had defeated repression, the economy had declined since 1985, and the fall of the Berlin Wall had removed the Cold War case for apartheid.
This meant that negotiation offered the National Party its best chance to protect white interests, which it believed it could control.
However, De Klerk was also more open to reform than Botha, and secret talks with Mandela had begun in 1985.
The most significant result was therefore the start of negotiations that would end white minority rule.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Analyse the reasons why the tricameral constitution failed to win support between 1983 and 1989.

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the question into its parts and show how they connect
decodeKey.judgement: Which reason mattered most, and how they connect

modelPlan.thesis: The tricameral constitution failed because it excluded the African majority while trying to divide the opposition, which provoked a mass, non-racial movement and a township uprising that repression could not crush.
modelPlan.counter: The constitution did give coloureds and Indians some representation, which a minority accepted.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which reason mattered most? The exclusion of Africans, which turned the reform into a provocation.

segments.text: The tricameral constitution failed because it reformed apartheid without ending it.
It gave coloureds and Indians separate houses with little power and excluded Africans, and fewer than 20 per cent of coloured and Indian voters took part in 1984.
This meant that the reform won no legitimacy and united opponents in the UDF, so from 1984 the townships rose in revolt.
However, the government kept power through the state of emergency, so the constitution failed politically but not immediately.
The exclusion of Africans was therefore the decisive reason for its failure.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast the reasons for the end of authoritarian rule in South Africa and Argentina between 1976 and 1990.

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences throughout
decodeKey.factorOrTask: Reasons for the end of authoritarian rule
decodeKey.judgement: Which reasons were shared, and which decided each case?

modelPlan.thesis: In both states economic decline, mass protest and military setbacks undermined authoritarian rule, but Argentina's junta collapsed after a single defeat, whereas South Africa's government chose to negotiate after years of resistance, sanctions and the end of the Cold War.

arguments.claim: Similarity and difference: military setbacks (Cuito Cuanavale; the Falklands).
Difference: negotiation from strength versus collapse.

modelPlan.counter: Argentina's regime ended within about eighteen months of its defeat, while South Africa's resisted pressure for well over a decade.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which reason decided each case? Defeat in Argentina; the combination of pressures in South Africa.

segments.text: Both regimes were weakened by the same kinds of pressure, but they ended in different ways.

In South Africa the 1985 debt crisis and the township uprising coincided with defeat at Cuito Cuanavale in 1988, whereas in Argentina wage freezes left real wages around 40 per cent lower before the Falklands defeat of 1982.
This meant that both governments lost the ability to rule by force alone, so each had to give way to demands for change.

However, Argentina's junta fell into disrepute after one military defeat, while South Africa's National Party negotiated from a position it believed it could control, after the end of the Cold War removed its Western protectors.
Authoritarian rule therefore ended for similar reasons in both states, but defeat caused a collapse in Argentina, while a combination of pressures produced a negotiated change in South Africa.
